zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check, after independent scan reading: the supplied *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan-based transcription and English notes are this reviewer's work; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

lines.note: Qinnen is explained as recent years, literally years near at hand. The damaged initial is Q, not OCR D, and Chicaqi supplies the expected 'near'; the Portuguese continues pouco across the row boundary.
Completes pouco and says that those years passed only a short time ago. The historical spelling paſſarão is retained, not converted to a modern past-tense spelling.

The entry concerns sinews and flesh. Enlargement shows Sugi, with a damaged u and a clear g, rather than OCR Sagi; the form is retained as printed rather than regularized to modern suji. Xiximura supplies the flesh component.
Carne completes the paired Portuguese gloss 'sinews and flesh'; it is a short continuation of Qinnicu, not an independent entry.
Nixiqino fucuro identifies a brocade bag. The headword's long-o mark points downward, and the Portuguese begins describing a bag made from fine fabric.

runs.text: na, como brocadilho, em que ſe metem couſas

lines.note: Completes fina and compares the material to brocade; the bag is used to put things in. The relative clause continues to specify their importance on the next row.
The contents are things of importance. This finishes the brocade-bag definition without adding any new Japanese material.
Qinô means yesterday, directly matched by Ontem. Its upward circumflex is distinct from the caron on Qinnǒ above.
Qinomi is tree fruit. The first letter is an upright Q with its descending tail, not an italic O detached from the headword.
Chicaqi fotori explains the nearby surroundings, and Perto gives 'near'. The italic Vt introduces an example of being nearby.
Qinpenni aru means that something is close by. The tilde in algũa is over u; the Japanese headword and its locative ending belong together.
Ou jũto adds 'or adjacent' to the preceding explanation. The abbreviation tilde is preserved rather than expanding the Portuguese word.
This Qinpenxu entry concerns personal attendants who serve someone directly. The source's tight Osque is retained; the object of their service follows below.

runs.text: ſenhor, ou andão à ſua ilharga.

lines.note: The attendants serve a lord or remain at his side. Ilharga supplies the physical 'side' image behind the close-service sense.
A separate identically spelled headword is glossed as neighbours. It should not be merged with the preceding definition of a lord's attendants.
Chicaqi catauara explains a nearby place or vicinity. The following example illustrates location, unlike the distinct resisting/prohibiting sense of the next Qinpǒ entry.
Qinpǒni aru means being nearby or adjacent. The long-o mark and attached ni agree with the immediately preceding location entry.
This homograph is explained through restraining and defending, then translated as resisting. Fuxegu is the historical spelling corresponding to fusegu; it is not a faulty long-s reading.
The example urges firm resistance against an enemy. The repeated word reads qinpǒ, not OCR qiupǒ, and xeyo is the imperative; the Portuguese verb continues on the next row.

runs.text: ti bem ao voßo inimigo prejudicial.

lines.note: Completes Reſiſti and translates the exhortation as resisting one's harmful enemy well. The printed voßo is preserved rather than expanded to a different s sequence.

Firugayeri supplies the idea of turning over, which the Portuguese renders as turning or overturning. The abbreviated second form u is retained exactly despite the fuller form a modern reader might expect.
Uoluer completes reuoluer, 'turn over'. The upright S. is the written-usage label and does not belong to the italic verb. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Aqino caje explains an autumn wind. The long-u mark is retained, and the final upright S. marks written usage rather than contributing to the Portuguese definition. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Certa aue como galinha do mato que

lines.note: Qinqei names a bird compared here to a wild hen. The damaged second vowel is i, not OCR u; the next row locates the bird in China, without establishing a modern species in this transcription.
This completes the bird description by saying that it occurs in China. China is part of the Portuguese gloss, not an embedded Japanese word.
Qinqet denotes splendid royal palaces. Its final t is retained as the printed checked ending rather than expanded to a modern Japanese syllable.

runs.text: Couſas que ſe prohibem, ou a que hum

lines.note: Qinqi first denotes things prohibited or avoided. The second relative clause continues into the explanation of personal aversion on the following row.

runs.text: tem aſco por lhe ſerem prejudiciaes pera o eſta-

lines.note: The avoidance is attributed to things being harmful to the stomach or health. The scan supports eſta- before mago, so the historical or anomalous vowel is not silently changed to modern estômago.
Mago completes the printed eſtamago; ſaude broadens the reference to health. These remain parts of the taboo/avoidance definition.
This separate Qinqi entry is a gold vessel, explained literally by Coganeno vtçuuamono. Initial v and the doubled u sequence belong to the printed Japanese spelling.
De ouro completes 'a vessel of gold'. The short continuation must remain separate from the adverbial entry below.
The repeated Chicaxi explains nearness, with Adu. identifying adverbial use. The following example shifts the proximity specifically to time: in the near future.

runs.text: Da qui a pouco tempo. Vt,

lines.note: The Portuguese narrows 'near' to a short time from now. Qinqinni begins the Japanese example and continues with the speaker's intended departure below.
Macari tatǒzu expresses an intended departure, translated as 'in a few days I will depart'. The historical prospective ending is retained rather than replaced by a modern verb form.
Partirei completes the first-person future statement. This short row belongs to the temporal example of Qinqin.
Cotono qiocu identifies a musical tune for the koto. The headword begins with roman Q, not OCR italic O; musica is divided after mu-.
Completes musica and specifies instrumental performance. Tanger here supplies playing an instrument, not a separate Japanese form.
Coganeno fana means golden flowers, rendered here as roses of gold. The metallic sense is distinct from the short-lived flower named by the following homograph.
The example describes placing golden flowers on a fence and crystal at the doors. The line ends with the full Japanese ſuixǒ; its object particle continues on the next row without an invented hyphen.
The opening uo completes the crystal phrase, and tçuranetari describes arranging it in a row. The Portuguese begins the corresponding account of golden roses placed on the hedge.
The translation concludes that the doors were made of crystal. This completes the ornamental example under the gold-flower sense of Qinqua.
This Qinqua is explained as the flower of asagao. The Portuguese merely calls it a flower of that name and continues the description below; it is not the golden ornament of the previous entry.

runs.text: da que não dura mais que tè ſair o ſol.

lines.note: Completes chamada and describes the flower as lasting only until sunrise. The statement is the dictionary's own description, not an independently imposed botanical identification.
Coganeno camuri explains a golden crown. Camuri is retained in the historical form shown, not modernized to kanmuri.
Qinrai means recently or in these recent times. The scan shows r rather than OCR t in the headword, consistent with Chicai coro and the temporal gloss.
The alternative explanation is 'a short time ago'. This completes Qinrai and does not belong to the textile entry below.

runs.text: Certa laya de brocadilho da china.

lines.note: Qinran names a kind of Chinese brocade. The final character is n, not the extra ni produced by OCR; the printed lowercase china is retained.
Qinren is described as rich mats or screens hung up for display. The definition itself supplies the hanging function; no more specific modern furnishing is imposed.
Qinri is equated with Dairi and glossed as the ruler's palace. Dairi is a Japanese synonym, not an embedded term within the Portuguese explanation.
Chicaqi tonari explains proximity or neighbouring location. The example on the next row applies the word to nearby notable flowers.
Qinrinno meiqua means notable flowers in the neighbourhood. The scan includes a paragraph mark before the example that the OCR omitted.
The relative clause says that the flowers are nearby. This completes the example under Qinrin rather than introducing another sense.
Coganeno ſacazzuqi identifies a golden drinking cup. The Portuguese offers two cup terms, dividing copo after co-.
Po completes copo, followed by 'of gold'. This short continuation closes the gold-cup definition.
Qinsǒ is first equated with Qizu, a wound. The next sense begins the Portuguese word for surgery, divided after Su-, and extends to the practitioner.

runs.text: rugia, ou ſurgião q̃ cura feridas. ¶

lines.note: Completes Surugia and adds a surgeon who treats wounds. The repeated Japanese Qinsǒ begins at the right edge and is genuinely hyphenated here.
Together with Qin- above, the example names a person who practices surgery. The Portuguese Surgião directly identifies that practitioner.

runs.text: O estar recolhido dentro de caſa ſem

lines.note: Qinſocu denotes remaining confined or withdrawn inside one's house. The qualification 'without going out' is completed below.
The example Qinſocu ſuru expresses staying indoors without going out. Vt is part of the italic explanatory apparatus, while the Japanese example is roman.
Qinſu is equated with Cogane and translated simply as gold. Neither an additional monetary sense nor a modern spelling is inserted.
Dairino niua identifies the palace courtyard or garden. The Portuguese starts Pateo, with a clear capital P, correcting OCR Fateo.
The gloss continues with the ruler's garden beds or planted area. Alegretes is preserved as the printed Portuguese term rather than replaced by a modern garden word.
Qintet combines gold and iron, explicitly supplied by Cogane and curogane. The following example contrasts their values rather than describing an alloy.
The example says that gold and iron do not have the same value. The initial of vonajǔ is read as the printed v; the negative xezu belongs to the historical Japanese construction.

runs.text: Ouro, & ferro não tem o meſmo preço.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly confirms the contrast: gold and iron do not have the same price. This anchors the value comparison in the preceding Japanese sentence.
Firugayeri tauoru describes turning over and falling. The Portuguese similarly combines turning with cair, divided after ca-.
Ir completes cair, 'fall'. The separate upright S. marks written usage, rather than being part of the italic infinitive. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Certa laya de Mochis redondos com

lines.note: Qinton is described as a kind of round Mochis. Enlargement supports Mochis rather than OCR Molbis; the Japanese food name occurs within the Portuguese explanation and takes a Portuguese plural ending.
The cakes are said to contain sugar. The printed historical aſucar is retained without adding a cedilla from modern orthography.
Qinu is a piece of fine or thin silk fabric. It is distinct from the following Qin v, despite their similar unaccented letters.
Qin v is equated with Nichirin and translated as the sun. The visibly separated v is preserved; it is not merged into the silk headword Qinu above.
Qinuguinu is a poetic expression for parting, equated with Vacare. Apartamento here means separation, not a modern residential apartment; the initial P. is the poetic label.
Qeccôna iye explains splendid houses. The printed Qinuocu is retained without changing its internal u to suit an expected modern romanization.
The houses are described as rich as well as beautiful. This completes the Portuguese adjective-and-noun phrase begun above.

runs.text: Paos com que batem as peças de ſeda,

lines.note: Qinuta is described here through the wooden implements used to beat silk cloth. The terminal mark is a comma, not the OCR period, continuing the list of fabrics below.
The continuation adds cangas and nonos to the fabrics beaten with these implements. The historical textile names are preserved rather than replaced with the generic Portuguese panos.

runs.text: Caſa onde ſe fazem, ou tecem peças

lines.note: Qinuya is a place where silk fabrics are made or woven. The Portuguese description concerns production rather than explicitly defining a retail shop.
This finishes the description as fine or thin pieces of silk. It belongs to the workshop entry, not the following textile name.
This Qinxa names a kind of thin fabric. Although a dark blot crosses delgadas, the surviving letters support the word; the opening headword is roman Q, not italic O.
This homograph means gold sand, explicitly explained by Coganeno iſago. The Portuguese Area is retained as printed rather than modernized to areia.
Qinxẽ denotes a golden fan, with the final nasal abbreviation preserved. The Japanese explanation uses vǒgui; the Portuguese describes a gilded fan.
Coganeno jeni identifies gold coins. The full -en ending distinguishes this printed headword from the abbreviated fan entry immediately above.
Qinxenqua names a kind of flower, described by the dictionary as a type of rose. A modern botanical species is not supplied from the headword alone.
The paired Japanese words are metal and stone. The Portuguese likewise uses the broader Metal here, rather than the narrower gold gloss seen in neighbouring entries.
Coganeno ſuricuzzu identifies gold scrapings or filings. The Portuguese offers powder or filings and divides limaduras after lima-.
Completes limaduras and begins the example 'although gold dust is precious'. Two adjacent t types are visible in tattoxito, correcting OCR tatoxito; iyedomo is divided across the physical rows.
The example continues: when gold dust enters the eye, it becomes an obstruction to sight. The Portuguese translation starts O ouro, divided after ou-.

runs.text: ro em pò poſtoque he muito estimado, toda-

lines.note: Completes ouro and states the concession: gold in powder form is highly valued. Todavia is divided at the edge as the translation turns to the contrasting consequence.

runs.text: uia caindo nos olhos cega, ou faz ſe neuoa dos

lines.note: The dictionary's comparison says that entering the eyes nevertheless blinds or becomes a mist over them. The historical spelling neuoa and the printed separation faz ſe are preserved.
Olhos completes the phrase about a mist over the eyes. This is the last continuation of the gold-dust example.
Coganeno ito identifies gold thread. This Qinxi entry concerns material, not the prohibition sense of the next homograph.
The Japanese explanation combines restraining and stopping, matching prohibition. The opening letter is a damaged Q, not the OCR G.
Qinxi ſuru is the verbal example, 'to prohibit'. The paragraph mark introduces the example within the same entry.
Chicaqi xinca describes a close retainer. The weak initial retains the tail of Q, correcting OCR C; the Portuguese specifies whose personal servant is meant on the next row.
Rey completes 'the king's personal servant'. The separate Ddd signature and Qinxit catchword formerly attached by OCR have been moved into furniture zones, not discarded or counted as body text.
